1.1.1 :115 IHEC Staff (8 females and 107 male) were trained in Logistics Management; 67 IHEC Staff (10 female and 57 male) were trained in Data Management; and 57 IHEC Staff, all male, were trained in Election Security
1.1.2 : 1. OEA organized a 5-day study visit for the IHEC Board of Commissioners to the Republic of South Africa as part of the commitment made by the UNAMI towards supporting the IHEC in the strengthening of its institutional and management capacity through the provisioning of out-of-country experience sharing. The delegation comprised the IHEC Vice Chair and three members of the Board of Commissions. The Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) of the Republic of South Africa is regarded by international analysts as advanced and highly experienced in many aspects of electoral processes. The objective of the study visit was to enable the IHEC delegation to learn from the gains of the Republic of South Africa and explore international standards and best practices in election management with a view to enhancing the credibility of electoral processes in Iraq. The study visit provided a learning opportunity for the IHEC Board of Commissioners on the legal framework, IEC structure, strategic and operational planning, voter registration, and electoral systems in South Africa. During the study visit, the IHEC delegation also observed polling day operations in a by-election in the Limpopo Province of South Africa. 2. Within the South-South Cooperation, UNAMI OEA supported the exchange between IHEC (Iraq) and the Office of Electoral Commissioner (Mauritius) to share experiences on their recent electoral cycles. From 19-25 November, the IHEC delegation composed of five of the IHEC BoC members and four of the UNAMI OEA staff joined the study visit the Mauritius where they visited the electoral management bodies of Mauritius. The visit included a two-day workshop with OEC Operations, a meeting with the Supreme Court of Mauritius, and a visit to the President of Mauritius. The delegation engaged in discussions about the electoral operations, stakeholders’ engagement, strategic planning, EMB management, and an in-depth overview of the last electoral cycles in each country: Iraq (2021), and Mauritius (2019). The hosting institutions shared the overall challenges, legal changes, stakeholders’ engagement, and operational procedures adopted.

2.2.1 : Two policies and procedures that were gender mainstreamed achieved. OEA prepared an advisory on Seat Allocation / Women Quota, to ensure that women quota is applied. The Constitution and Election Laws provides for and guarantees the minimum quota of 83 women seats in the Council of Representatives, however, it also allows for more women to be allocated seats, if they are elected. Despite of the fact that nothing in the electoral legislation can be construed as a limitation to allocate to women more than one seat in each constituency, there was a tendency to interpret the women quota as a ceiling. Thus, as to ensure women quota is not a ceiling, OEA provided technical assistance including preparation of an advisory based on the national electoral legislation, international standards and best practices and participation of IHEC Legal Committee during preparation of Regulation on Seat Allocation. Technical assistance provided by OEA ensured adoption of the Seat Regulation with interpretation of the women quota in accordance with the international standards and best practice. The members of the integrated gender and elections task force (including OEA, UNAMI Gender, UNDP and UN Women) maintained regular liaison with IHEC counterparts, including the female IHEC Commissioner, in the run up to the elections. OEA prepared fact sheets on women quota and disseminated through the UNAMI website and social media account. UNAMI OEA together with the Office of Political Affairs (OPA), facilitated a series of consultative meetings among political parties, alliances, independent candidates, and the Office of the President, for the preparation of the Charter of Honor (Electoral Code of Conduct). Further to this the UNAMI Office of Gender Affairs introduced the necessary revision of the language to advance women candidate’s protection in the Charter of Honor.
